apparatus.basis: Standard running header of the Kephalaia is ⲙ̄ⲡⲥⲁⲍ 'Of the Teacher.' Here the editor reads ⲙ̄ⲡⲉ + [ⲁⲍ] — the visible ⲡⲉ is anomalous (possibly scribal/orthographic for ⲡⲥ); restored as the conventional running title.
Lycopolitan ⲭⲛ̄ ⲙ̄ⲡⲓⲛⲉⲩ = Sahidic ϫⲓⲛ ⲙ̄ⲡⲓⲛⲁⲩ 'from this hour' — standard time-marker idiom (cf. accumulated ⲡⲓⲛⲉⲩ 'this moment').
Editor's restoration of single letter completing the standard form ⲛ̄ⲕⲉⲥⲁⲡ 'another time/turn' (cf. accumulated vocab).
ⲟⲩⲛ̄ †ⲱⲃ 'there is a matter' standard Coptic existential introducing the disciple's pending question; the disciple's question construction is completed by ⲍ ⲙⲙⲁⲕ 'with you' in the next line.
ⲍⲁ-ⲙⲙⲁⲕ 'with you' — standard formula in disciple-question construction 'there is a matter with you, my Lord.'
Editor's restoration of single letter completing ⲡⲁⲭⲁⲓⲥ 'my Lord' (Lyc reflex of ⲡϫⲟⲉⲓⲥ; in accumulated vocab).
Causative on ⲟⲩⲱⲛϩ̄ 'manifest' = Lyc ⲁⲧⲟⲩⲛⲟⲩⲓ̈ⲉ (in accumulated vocab as 'make known/reveal'). Standard disciple-petition formula.

apparatus.english: the matter that I have asked
apparatus.basis: ⲡⲍⲱⲃ 'the matter' (Lyc for ⲡϩⲱⲃ) + ⲉⲧⲁⲓ̈-ⲱⲛⲧ 'which I have asked,' standard disciple-question formula (cf. accumulated ⲱⲛⲧ ⲁⲣⲁ⸗ 'inquire about').
Continues the relative perfect from previous line: ⲉⲧⲁⲓ̈-ⲱⲛⲧ-ⲕ ⲁⲣⲁϩ 'which I have asked you about' — standard formula closing the disciple's petition.
Standard chapter-opening formula ⲡⲁⲭⲉ ⲡⲁⲡⲟⲥⲧⲟⲗⲟⲥ 'said the Apostle' (cf. accumulated ⲡⲁⲡⲟⲥⲧⲟⲗⲟⲥ, ⲡⲧⲁⲭⲉ); the restoration ⲡⲟⲥⲧⲟⲗⲟⲥ continues into line 5.

notes.decision: Translated as 'the body.' The form ⲡⲉⲱⲙⲁ is anomalous; standard Coptic is ⲡⲥⲱⲙⲁ (Greek σῶμα). Most likely either (a) a scribal slip omitting the ⲥ-, or (b) a Lycopolitan dialectal variant ⲡⲉ-ⲱⲙⲁ where ⲱⲙⲁ reflects a reduced form. The reading 'body' is required by the parallel ⲡⲥⲱⲙⲁ ⲧⲛⲧⲁⲛⲧ ⲁⲡⲕⲁⲍ 'the body is likened to the land' in line 7, which is the explicit topic of the kephalaion.

The verb is a causative on ⲟⲩⲱⲛϩ̄/ⲧⲟⲩⲛⲟⲥ 'manifest, raise up to view' (per accumulated vocabulary entry ⲁⲧⲟⲩⲛⲟⲩⲓ̈ⲉ 'make known/reveal'). Translated 'make known forth.' This is the standard disciple-petition verb in the Kephalaia for requesting an apostolic exposition.

notes.coptic_form: ⲡⲥⲱⲙⲁ ⲧⲛⲧⲁⲛⲧ ⲁⲡⲕⲁⲍ ⲉⲣⲉ ⲛⲓⲙⲉⲗⲟⲥ ... ⲉⲩⲧⲛⲧⲁⲛⲧ ⲁⲛⲱⲏⲛ
notes.decision: The framing direct correspondence: 'the body IS likened to the land' (using ⲧⲛⲧⲁⲛⲧ qualitative — cf. accumulated entry). The members within it correspondingly IS likened to ⲛ̄ⲱⲏⲛ 'trees' (Lyc ⲡⲱⲏⲛ = ⲡϣⲏⲛ, in glossary). The kephalaion thus opens with a layered correspondential identification — body:land :: members:trees — preparing the parable that follows about which trees regrow when cut.

Parsed as ⲉ-ϣⲁ-ⲕ-ⲟⲛⲧⲟⲩ 'when one (habitually) plants/sets them' — agricultural verb in line with the tree-planting context. The ⲟⲛⲧ⸗ stem may reflect ⲡⲱⲛⲧ̄/ⲱⲛⲧ̄ 'set, place' (cf. tentative glossary entry ⲱⲛⲧⲟⲩ 'match/correspond them' but here in concrete agricultural register). Translated 'plants them' as the contextually required action; the verb governs the trees' subsequent sprouting and standing fast.

ⲱⲁⲧⲟⲩ from ϣⲱⲱⲧ 'cut, cut down' (in accumulated vocab as ϣⲱϩⲧ 'cutting'); ⲙⲁⲩⲣⲱⲧ negative habitual 'they do not grow.' The antithetical pair structures the parable: trees that regrow when cut versus trees that do not. This botanical taxonomy underlies the moral-anthropological teaching about which embodied desires can be eradicated and which persist.

Greek ἀκαθαρσία 'impurity, uncleanness' (Lyc plural ⲁⲕⲁⲫⲁⲣⲥⲓⲁ with ⲫ for θ — regular Lyc orthography). ⲛⲧⲟⲩⲁⲙ likely Lyc for 'of their food/eating' (ⲟⲩⲱⲙ 'eat'). The phrase 'in the impurities of their food/eating' fits the kephalaion's bodily-discipline register: the trees that regrow when cut are nourished by impure food, an image for the regrowing desires sustained by the unclean nourishment of the flesh.

Translated 'this flesh which is desire-arousing forth.' ⲗⲉϩⲗⲁϩⲧ is the qualitative of the desire-arousing root (per accumulated vocab entry ⲗⲉϩⲗⲁϩⲧ 'desire-arousing/lust-inciting'). The lust-inciting flesh is the ground of the regrowing-tree members of the body — the very desires that, when 'cut,' grow back from their impure root. Closes the kephalaion's botanical parable with the explicit naming of the corresponding moral-physical reality.
